description: Bizler Doğa Koleji 7.sınıf öğrencileriyiz. Müzik ve seslere olan ilgimizi bu proje ile birleştirmek istedik. Araştırmayı ve sorun çözmeyi severiz. Dünya daki farklı yer şekillerine meraklıyız. Takım çalışması ve işbirliğine açık bir grubuz.
summary:
We are going to show that sound isn't just for listening to music. It can actually carry incredible information!
By combining nine amazing geographical locations in our country with audio engineering, we have officially created 'audible geography'! While doing this, we were inspired by the soundification concept of the NASA Earth Information Center. We created a coding system using frequencies (Hz), sound levels (dB), and different instruments for these locations.
"We took color and brightness codes from items 5114, 5067, and 5193 in NASA's SVS archive, and turned them straight into sound frequencies and volumes. Because of this, our visually impaired friends or anyone who hasn't seen these places can experience mountains, plains, seas, canyons, lakes, and forests through sound. 
Plus, we can even learn about humidity, slope, wind, soil structure, and nature's liveliness using sound!" As the TerraSonics  the model we built could evolve into an auditory navigation device or a talking atlas in the future.
details:
Türkiye's Music Box

In this study, our aim as the TerraSonics group is to demonstrate that sound is not only an aesthetic musical medium, but also an information carrier capable of conveying any data and geography. Within the scope of the study, one of our primary objectives is to enable visually impaired individuals and friends who have never seen these regions in our country to vividly visualize the geographical characteristics of a given region in their minds, without the need for any visual stimuli, solely through the frequency height of sound (for example, we symbolized steep slopes with 2–8 kHz high-pitched string attacks) and the propagation pattern of amplitude (we matched canyon and lake depths with continuous bass below 60 Hz).

Another goal of ours is to promote our country. We blended the geological and topographic parameters of nine geographical locations that we consider significant for our country with the principles of sound engineering and acoustic theory, thereby constructing an "audible geography."

Inspired by the data sonification philosophy adopted by NASA’s Earth Information Center (EIC), our study codes designated geographical structures using rules of frequency distributions (Hz), amplitude dynamics (dB), resonance, and instrumentation:

  • SVS ID: 5114 — Global Elevation and Bathymetry was used to directly translate the elevation of the Anatolian plateau, the heights of the Taurus mountain range, and canyon depressions into frequency via pixel brightness (luminance).
  • SVS ID: 5193 was used to convert the moisture density of the Eastern Black Sea (Ayder) and the precipitation regime feeding river basins into rhythm.
  • SVS ID: 5067 — ECOSTRESS & MODIS Thermal Spectrum was mapped to the balance between bass drones and tense high harmonics.

The TerraSonics acoustic matrix is designed to convert the color and brightness parameters of the SRTM/GEBCO Digital Elevation Model data layers (SVS #5114, SVS #5067, SVS #5193) from the NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS) archive directly into frequency (Hz) and amplitude (dB) rules.

In creating the program, photo editors, the Flutter coding framework, music editing applications, and the Suno AI tool were used. Additionally, a mini quiz was added to the study to create an entertaining interaction. Based on geographical structures, our study features nine regions: Ayder Plateau, Erzincan Dark Canyon, the Taurus Mountains, Çukurova, the Aegean Sea, Lake Tuz, İğneada Floodplain Forests, Lake Van, and Mount Nemrut.

Regional Sonification Breakdowns

1. Ayder Plateau

High-pitched high frequencies (2 kHz – 8 kHz) driving the main melody; a slightly raspy, rhythmic, string-like texture via the kemençe (a bowed string instrument) for mid frequencies (500 Hz – 2 kHz); percussion elements like the tambourine (def) for rhythm; and bass layers (60 Hz – 250 Hz) supporting the rhythm without overpowering it were utilized. It features a high and compressed amplitude structure that keeps the energy alive from start to finish. Dense frequencies above 3 kHz represent sharp humidity and steep slopes, while high foggy plateaus reached via rugged roads are complemented by irregularly spaced beats and instantaneous accelerations combined with intense bass. Sudden decibel leaps also complete the rhythm.

2. Erzincan Dark Canyon

The weight of the river silently passing hundreds of meters below the canyon was simulated by heavy bass drones between 20 Hz – 150 Hz representing its discharge rate. Cello and double bass aimed to provide density with continuous resonance below 60 Hz. Treble frequencies (4 kHz and above) were intentionally suppressed to create the sensation of being heard from inside a well. High frequencies and muffled mid tones were used to represent the limestone cliffs. Wide wavelengths that slowly rise and take a long time to decay are dominant.

3. The Taurus Mountains

High-frequency, continuously forward-pushing beats and accelerations in the 2 kHz – 8 kHz range represent the steep slopes of goat paths; compressed high amplitude represents the summit; mid frequencies (500 Hz – 2 kHz) are supported by rhythmic percussion strikes; and the bass layer in the 60 Hz – 250 Hz range aims to convey the mass of the mountain. Sudden decibel leaps and high string entries represent the impassable nature of these massive mountain ranges preventing passage into inner regions due to their structure.

4. Çukurova

Using the def, dümbelek, and bendir, the flood discharge of the rivers feeding the plain and the fertile alluvial soil layer accumulated by the Seyhan and Ceyhan rivers over thousands of years were simulated with balanced bass frequencies of 60 Hz – 200 Hz. The fluid and syncopated beats in the piece represent the flood flows of the Seyhan and Ceyhan rivers shaping the delta plain. Uninterrupted agricultural lands on the plain were complemented with compressed high amplitude.

5. The Aegean Sea

Fluid frequency shifts and glissandos represent meanders and grabens; fluctuating amplitude and harmony above 3 kHz represent mountains extending perpendicular to the sea; syncopated yet oscillating rhythms represent Horst-Graben depressions; while mid frequencies (500 Hz – 2.5 kHz) enriched with the ney and kaval (reed flutes) aim to represent its long coastlines.

6. Lake Tuz

High frequencies in the 3 kHz – 8 kHz range represent salt crystals through plucked string plectrum strikes and high-pitched percussion chimes. While mid frequencies (500 Hz – 2.5 kHz) represent the steppe plains, an open dynamic range where individual plectrum strikes can be heard clearly dominates the amplitude.

7. İğneada Floodplain Forests

The forest structure is represented by high-frequency natural sounds of different species in the 4 kHz – 10 kHz range; leaf rustling with light percussion; guitar arpeggios and soft, rhythmic finger taps represent the reedbeds on the forest floor; and fluid, clear arpeggios with treble frequencies above 4 kHz represent plant diversity such as ash, alder, and lagoons, while the amplitude of the piece maintains a wide dynamic structure.

8. Lake Van

A robust and deep bass layer with lower frequencies (50 Hz – 150 Hz) represents the volcanic basin formed by extinct volcanoes; mid-frequency whistles and mey represent Akdamar and Çarpanak islands; plectrum strikes above 3 kHz represent the soda-rich, crystallized lake water structure; and percussion strikes and hazy breath attacks are used to signify the internal sea-like nature of the region.

9. Mount Nemrut

High frequencies in the 2.5 kHz – 7 kHz range are provided by string instrument strikes. Mid frequencies (400 Hz – 2 kHz) are enhanced with mey timbres alongside other wind instruments. A robust and grounded bass layer in the 50 Hz – 200 Hz range was used to convey the majesty of the massive stone tumulus and statues at an altitude of 2,150 meters. While percussion strikes are kept distinct and crisp, background strings and wind instrument elongations are intended to create an echo effect across a wide valley.
